newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sony Music earnings fall due to lack of big hits.
newsitem.headline: Sony Music earnings fall due to lack of big hits.

text.p: Sony Music Entertainment (Japan) Inc., the recording company of Michael Jackson and Bruce Springsteen, said Wednesday its earnings in the year to March 31 fell sharply due to a shortage of big hits.
Japan's major record company, affiliated with Sony Corp., said its parent sales totalled 103.1 billion yen ($824 million) in 1996/97, down 10.0 percent from the previous year.
Sony Music said its current profit fell 45.6 percent to 11.4 billion yen ($91.2 million). Current profit is pre-tax and includes losses and gains on investments.
"In popular music, the number of big selling products was less than in the previous year," the company said.

Sales from its Japanese repertoire, which accounts for more than half of the company's business, were depressed 6.5 percent from the previous year due to a reduction in newly released recordings and a lack of big hits.
The non-Japanese repertoire sales showed a 12.2 percent decline in 1996/97, despite the popularity of some of its artists, such as Celine Dion and Jamiroquai.
The European pop band Jamiroquai sold more than one million copies of its new album, "Travelling without Moving," in Japan.
Despite a decline in pop hits, sales of classical music showed a steady increase, Sony Music said.
Sony's custom manufacturing division was the only product group that posted an increase in sales in 1996/97.
Net sales rose 4.1 percent due mainly to robust demand for CD-ROMs for software used in Sony Computer Entertainment Inc.'s hit home video game machine, PlayStation.
For the current business year to the end of March 1998, the company forecasts sales of 111.2 billion yen ($889 million) and a current profit of 11.9 billion yen ($95.2 million).
